newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac sees growth, tax cuts for "dynamic" French.
newsitem.headline: Chirac sees growth, tax cuts for "dynamic" French.

text.p: Little-loved President Jacques Chirac, donning a more optimistic, can-do style, pledged faster economic growth and lower taxes on Tuesday and praised his fellow citizens' "dynamism" in a televised New Year address.

"1996 was a difficult year for many of us. I know," said Chirac whose popularity, like that of his centre-right Prime Minister Alain Juppe, has slumped to record lows in the face of austerity policies, rising unemployment and labour conflicts.

The tone and content of the president's message, broadcast before the evening news, contrasted with his last television appearance in which he criticised French people's "conservatism" in resisting many of the government's reforms.

"Our country is changing, moving, calling itself into question. Beyond blockages and conservatisms which exist here and there, I see evidence of dynamism and vitality," said Chirac, flanked by a French tricolour and a European Union flag.

"1997 will really be that of jobs for the young, as I have wished, if all commit themselves with determination and imagination," he said in his second New Year message since his election in early 1995.

Chirac's appeals for understanding of austerity policies in a lengthy interview on December 12 had failed to lift his low popularity significantly, with he and Juppe only slightly up in recent opinion polls.
Opposition Socialists derided him as apparently powerless given his criticism of the French for resisting many of his reforms.
In his New Year address, Chirac did not name Juppe but singled out the government's welfare and unemployment subsidy reforms as evidence that France was forging ahead.
He urged parties in labour disputes "not to harm the general interest in the name of individual interests, and not to expect everything from the State".

The government has caved in repeatedly in labour disputes in recent weeks, granting early retirement, shorter working hours and wage hikes for example to truckers who set up blockades on main roads across the country.
"Our growth has been too weak this year to bring unemployment down, which is my main objective. But our growth is taking off again and will be stronger in 1997," Chirac said.
"It is up to the government to free up energies...By simplifying rules, formalities and paper-work. By speeding up tax cuts which have been launched, as you will note in coming months," he said.
Unemployment hit a record 12.7 percent in November, resuming its steady rise after a surprise drop in October, and economists said the peak was still some way off.
The number of unemployed rose by 20,700 last month, after a 12,000 decline in October, to reach 3,121,500 after adjusting for seasonal variations, the Labour Ministry said on Monday.
This rise pushed the jobless rate up from 12.6 percent of the workforce in October.

For the government, languishing at record lows in opinion polls, the figures make its pledge to cut unemployment ever harder to fulfill as it tries to rein in spending to meet deficit criteria for joining a single European currency in 1999.
